items.title: UK GDPR, Article 28: Processor
items.quote: the controller shall use only processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures
items.why: The binding rule where a supplier handles personal data: due diligence before appointment, a contract, and the same obligations passed down to any sub-processor. It covers data protection, not the security of the model or interface as such.

items.title: Supply chain security guidance. I. Understand the risks
items.quote: Until you have a clear picture of your supply chain, it will be very hard to establish any meaningful control over it.
items.why: Source of the quotation. The first three of 12 principles: understand what needs protecting, know who the suppliers are and what their security looks like, and understand the risk the chain poses. Tells organisations to decide how far down the chain they need to look. Not written for AI.

items.title: Supply chain security guidance. III. Check your arrangements
items.quote: Require those suppliers who are key to the security of your supply chain, via contracts, to provide upward reporting of security performance
items.why: The contractual side: upward reporting, a right to audit that is exercised, assurance requirements such as penetration tests or certification, and performance indicators. The guidance itself notes a right to audit may not be possible for a cloud service.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: System Operators shall communicate their intention to update models to End-users in an accessible way prior to models being updated.
items.why: The AI-specific supply chain expectations: secure supply chain processes, a documented justification and risk assessment for poorly documented components, re-running evaluations on released models, notice before a model is updated, and an inventory of assets with their interdependencies. Voluntary.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: Gain assurance that supplier information is routinely assessed, proportionate to their level of risk
items.why: What the board is asked to assure: routine, proportionate assessment of suppliers and resilience to risks from the supply chain and business partners. Voluntary; designed for medium and large organisations.

items.title: Cyber Assessment Framework, Principle A4: Supply chain
items.locator: Principle A4 description and guidance; version 4.0, reviewed 6 August 2025
items.quote: If an organisation relies on third parties (such as outsourced or cloud-based technology services) it remains accountable for the protection of any essential function.
items.why: States plainly that accountability stays with the organisation using the service. Asks for contractual provisions that protect what the function depends on. Written for operators of essential functions.

items.title: Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Home Office
items.quote: Just over one in ten businesses said they reviewed the risks posed by their immediate suppliers (15%)
items.why: Source of the figure: 15% reviewed immediate suppliers and 6% the wider supply chain; 48% and 24% among large businesses. The summary of the same report words the 6% as 'under one in ten', section 3.10 as 'around one in twenty'; the percentage is the same. About cyber risk from suppliers generally, not AI suppliers.

items.title: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Sections 'Overview' and 'Latest'; page last updated 18 November 2025
items.quote: The government introduced the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill to Parliament for its first reading on 12 November 2025.
items.why: Status of proposed law. The page says the Bill had completed second reading and committee stage in the Commons. Parliament's own Bill page refused automated access on the date checked, so the current stage was not confirmed there; a title search of legislation.gov.uk returned no Act. Treat as not yet law.

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation: government response
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 5.2, Box 2 and section 5.2.1 (case study on liability across the supply chain)
items.quote: Developers of these systems currently face the least clear legal responsibilities.
items.why: Why assessment has to run upstream: the government's own analysis that existing law tends to place liability on the last actor in the chain, the deployer, while developers of the most capable general-purpose models have the least clear duties. A policy paper of the previous government; no legislation followed from it in the sources read.

items.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Appendix A, GOVERN function, category GV.SC (GV.SC-01 to GV.SC-10), PDF pages 22 to 23
items.quote: GV.SC-04: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality
items.why: International comparator. Ten outcomes for supply chain risk, including due diligence before a relationship begins, requirements in contracts, suppliers included in incident planning, and provisions for what happens after the agreement ends. Voluntary; not AI-specific.

items.title: Final Notice: Equifax Limited
items.quote: firms regulated by the Authority remain responsible for ensuring that all regulatory requirements are met
items.why: Enforcement decision on an unassessed dependency: the firm sent UK consumer data to its parent for processing and had no adequate framework for monitoring the parent's security; data on 13.8 million UK individuals was exposed and the penalty was £11,164,400. Shows that a supplier inside the same group still has to be assessed. Financial services; a 2017 breach; no AI system involved.

items.title: Software provider fined £3m following 2022 ransomware attack
items.locator: Opening summary and the paragraphs that follow it
items.quote: Hackers accessed certain systems of Advanced’s health and care subsidiary via a customer account that did not have multi-factor authentication (MFA).
items.why: Enforcement against a supplier acting as a data processor for the NHS and other healthcare providers: its security gaps disrupted services such as NHS 111 and exposed data on 79,404 people. The customer's exposure was the vendor's weakness. The regulator's statement was read, not the full penalty notice; settled by agreement.

items.title: SS2/21 Outsourcing and third party risk management
items.locator: Chapter 9 (Sub-outsourcing), paragraph 9.3; Chapter 5, paragraph 5.18; Chapter 10 (Business continuity and exit plans), paragraph 10.1
items.quote: It is important that firms have visibility of the supply chain
items.why: The fullest UK regulatory statement of the whole criterion: due diligence before signing, visibility of the supplier's own suppliers, and a documented, tested exit strategy for stressed and planned exits. November 2024 version, updating March 2021. Applies to PRA-regulated firms; other businesses can use it as a benchmark.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
items.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
items.quote: A third of all AI use cases are third-party implementations.
items.why: UK evidence on how much AI is bought in: a third of use cases, up from 17% in 2022, with the top three providers accounting for 73% of reported cloud providers and 44% of model providers. A survey of regulated financial firms, self-reported.

items.title: Understanding accountability in algorithmic supply chains
items.quote: algorithmic accountability discussions must consider supply chains and the difficult implications they raise for the governance and accountability of algorithmic systems
items.why: Peer-reviewed analysis by UK-based researchers (ACM FAccT 2023) of why AI built from several companies' services is hard to hold to account: responsibility is spread across actors and each can see only part of the chain. Conceptual, not empirical.

items.title: How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?
items.quote: when and how these models are updated over time is opaque
items.why: Evidence for reassessing when the model changes: the same hosted service gave markedly different results three months apart, for example 84% against 51% accuracy on one task. Preprint in the version read (revised 31 October 2023); two models from one provider in 2023, so the size of the effect will not carry over to other services.

items.title: BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain
items.quote: outsourced training introduces new security risks
items.why: The founding study of the model supply chain as a security risk: a model trained by someone else can pass the buyer's tests and still carry a hidden backdoor, which survives later retraining. Preprint (revised 2019); laboratory demonstrations on image classifiers, not large language models.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: GAI value chains involve many third-party components such as procured datasets, pre-trained models, and software libraries.
items.why: The AI-specific counterpart to the general NIST framework already listed: names untraceable third-party components as a risk in its own right and notes it can be hard to attribute a fault to any one source. Voluntary; a United States document on generative AI only.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 25: Responsibilities along the AI value chain
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: shall, by written agreement, specify the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance
items.why: Supply-chain assurance made contractual in law: the provider of a high-risk system and a third party supplying a model, tool or component must agree in writing the information and access needed for compliance. The Commission's copy of the EUR-Lex consolidated text as at 27 July 2026; paragraph 4 is marked AMENDED by the Digital Omnibus. Binds providers of high-risk systems, not deployers, and reaches UK firms only where the Act applies to them.
